draft.title: Government's economic aims
card: The government sets economic aims to raise living standards, which means how well off people are in terms of income, jobs and access to goods and services.
Growth
strong, steady growth in the economy, which means the total output of goods and services rises at a healthy pace without big swings.
Low unemployment
as many people as possible who want a job can find one.
Stable prices

prices rise only slowly and predictably, so households and businesses can plan ahead. A fair share of income is the fourth aim: it means that income is spread so that people on low incomes are not left far behind.
draft.remember: Growth, jobs, stable prices and a fair share of income all aim to lift living standards.

a.q: Which of these is an example of the aim of stable prices?
opts: Prices of most goods rise slowly and predictably
Wages rise faster than prices every single year
More people find full-time work in regional towns
Income is spread more evenly between households
a.why: Stable prices means prices rise only slowly and predictably. The option about jobs is the aim of low unemployment, and the option about income spread is the aim of a fair share of income.
a.clue: Think about what households need to plan ahead.

b.q: Many people in the town of Wagga lose their jobs when a large factory closes. Which government aim is most directly under threat?
opts: Low unemployment
Stable prices
Strong, steady growth
A fair share of income
b.why: Job losses on this scale mean more people who want work cannot find it, so the aim of low unemployment is most directly under threat. Growth and income spread may also be affected later, but the direct problem is jobs.
b.clue: Look at what people have lost first.

a.best: Prices of most goods rise slowly and predictably

problems.detail: The fourth aim, a fair share of income, is placed inside the 'Stable prices' bullet rather than on its own line, so a student could read it as part of stable prices instead of a separate aim.
